result:
I want to write about the moment right after the laundry is done.

The dryer hums and then sighs. The door pops open and a warm, slightly damp cloud rolls out. It smells like clean cotton and a little bit of the detergent I bought because the bottle was blue and the label promised "Mountain Breeze." There is no mountain in my life, just a fire escape and a neighbor who practices saxophone on Tuesdays.

I pull out the socks first because they always come out in pairs that aren't actually pairs. One is always hotter. I hold them up to the light and think about how strange it is that we put so much trust in machines to take care of the soft things. They tumble and beat and then we fold them into little squares that immediately get messy again.

My kitchen window is open a crack. The air is that specific early October air where it is cool enough for a sweater but the sun still has enough weight to warm the back of your neck. A pigeon lands on the ledge and looks at me like I owe it money. I don't give it bread because I read somewhere that bread is bad for them, which feels like a metaphor for a lot of good intentions.

I make tea I will not finish. I like the ritual more than the drinking. The kettle whistles, I pour, the steam fogs my glasses for three seconds. In that three seconds the world goes soft at the edges and I can pretend the to-do list on my fridge is just a series of words, not obligations.

There is a pen on the counter with no cap. I pick it up and write on the back of a grocery receipt: "the dryer is warm, the pigeon is judging me, the tea is cooling." That is the whole day, really. If you look closely enough, most days are made of three small observations stitched together.

Later I will put the laundry away and some of it will end up on the chair anyway. The socks will disappear into the laundry basket again by next week. The pigeon will be gone. The tea will be cold.

But for now the apartment smells like clean laundry and the sun is still on my neck. That is enough to write about.
